steps.action: Took the expected magnetite and hematite slip and twin systems and their temperature ranges from published laboratory experiments.
steps.quote: Experimental observations by Hennig-Michaeli and Siemes (1975)

steps.action: Named the gap: microstructural evidence of intracrystalline deformation (subgrains) is rare in naturally deformed magnetite and hematite.
steps.quote: subgrains have rarely been encountered in naturally deformed hematite

steps.action: Took the published topotaxial relation for magnetite-to-hematite replacement, hematite (0001) parallel to magnetite (111), as the expected relation.
steps.quote: parallelism of the basal (0001) planes of hematite to the octahedral (111) planes of magnetite

steps.action: Set the aims: the creep mechanisms of quartz and the Fe-oxides, and whether magnetite transformed topotaxially into hematite.
steps.quote: evaluate the possibility of a topotaxial transformation of magnetite into hematite

steps.action: Collected three meta-BIF samples within the Cauvery Shear System near Namakkal, recording a past deformation history known only from traces.
steps.quote: Three meta-BIF samples from the SGT were collected and examined.

steps.action: Prepared XZ thin sections and examined them by optical microscopy to identify the minerals and the deformation microstructures.
steps.quote: Polished thin sections, cut along the stretching lineation and perpendicular to the foliation (XZ-section)

steps.action: Acquired EBSD maps with an FE-SEM, indexed them in AZtec, and processed them in MTEX (cleaning, Voronoi grain reconstruction at a 10° threshold).
steps.quote: Electron backscattered diffraction (EBSD) data was then acquired from the polished surface using JEOL JSM-7100F FE-SEM

steps.action: Designed the analysis: CPO indices (J_ODF, M, mpfJ) from all points and from one point per grain, misorientation angle and axis analysis, and a tilt/twist/general classification of boundaries by the angle α.
steps.quote: we base our interpretations on the results of the former method

steps.action: Built a MTEX script for subgrain boundary trace analysis that derives slip plane normals and slip directions from sets of near-parallel tilt or twist boundaries.
steps.quote: the script developed for and used in this study to perform the subgrain boundary trace analysis

steps.action: Reported petrography, EBSD grain-size distributions of quartz and hematite, and quartz microstructures (deformation lamellae, BLG, GBM, subgrains, chessboard extinction) for each sample.
steps.quote: both mean and median of the quartz grain size distributions decrease from samples MA01 to MA03 to MA02

steps.action: Checked the bimodal EBSD quartz grain-size distribution of MA03 against optical microscopy.
steps.quote: as is also observed from optical microscopy

steps.action: Measured the CPOs of quartz, hematite and magnetite in all samples from the EBSD pole figures and strength indices.
steps.quote: The quartz grains exhibit well-defined CPOs

steps.action: Compared magnetite (111) CPOs with hematite (0001) CPOs per sample and grain by grain in MA02, against the expected topotaxial relation.
steps.quote: matches with those of (0001) of hematite

steps.action: Compared neighbour-pair misorientation angle distributions with the random-pair and theoretical (uniform) distributions as a null reference.
steps.quote: the misfit between the random and theoretical distributions is the highest for MA03

steps.action: Inferred magnetite slip systems from the subgrain boundary trace analysis of six grains with tilt boundaries.
steps.quote: Various slip systems are identified from these grains

steps.action: Mapped grain orientation spread (GOS) in MA02 and MA03 to compare the accumulated strain in hematite and magnetite.
steps.quote: the hematite grains are relatively more strained than the host magnetite grains

steps.action: Constrained deformation temperatures from the plagioclase/orthopyroxene and quartz microstructures, using published calibrations.
steps.quote: The presence of deformation lamellae in MA01 indicates low-grade conditions

steps.action: Posed two rivals for the bimodal quartz grain size of MA03: Zener pinning by secondary phases, or a precursor grain-size heterogeneity; neither was excluded.
steps.quote: the possibility of this grain-size variation being a precursor fabric in the BIF could not be refuted

steps.action: Inferred the active quartz slip systems from the low-angle misorientation axis distributions under tilt and twist assumptions, giving deformation over a wide temperature range.
steps.quote: The LAX orientations clearly suggest that the quartz grains in both MA02 and MA03 were deformed over a wide range of temperature

steps.action: Kept dislocation creep as the dominant deformation mechanism in quartz, from the non-random CPOs and crystallographically controlled misorientation axes.
steps.quote: validate dislocation creep as the dominant mechanism that accommodated intracrystalline deformation

steps.action: Inferred {111} twinning in magnetite from the ~60° neighbour-pair misorientation peaks about [111], implying ductile deformation below 400 °C.
steps.quote: This indicates that magnetite continued to deform in ductile regime below 400 °C

steps.action: Compared the magnetite slip planes and directions with those reported from laboratory experiments and the Hornstra slip-direction rule.
steps.quote: Subgrain boundary trace analysis conducted on the selected grains of MA02 confirm slip along {111}, {110}, and {100}

steps.action: Checked the boundary type of Grains 7 and 8 by comparing the PGA dispersion axes with the low-angle misorientation axes.
steps.quote: the dispersion axes, for both the cases, are nearly parallel (<5°) to the LAXs

steps.action: Rejected the twist interpretation of the α > 75° boundaries in Grains 7 and 8 in favour of tilt.
steps.quote: suggesting that these are more likely to be tilt boundaries

steps.action: Took from Yin et al. (2022) the prediction that a redox-independent replacement grows hematite (10-12) parallel to magnetite (110), as distinct from the redox relation.
steps.quote: redox independent transformations could cause

steps.action: Compared the magnetite and hematite CPO maxima against the redox and non-redox topotaxial predictions.
steps.quote: the maxima for [111] in magnetite and [0001] in hematite are indeed parallel

steps.action: Excluded the non-redox replacement because the (110) magnetite // (10-12) hematite relation is absent.
steps.quote: implying that the topotaxial replacement occurred via a redox reaction

steps.action: Kept the conclusions: dislocation creep in quartz and magnetite, multiple magnetite slip systems, redox topotaxial replacement along {111}, rapid recovery, and weak post-replacement deformation.
steps.quote: The well-developed CPOs along with low (<1°) GOS values suggest that the recovery processes were fast.

end.claim: Quartz and magnetite in the CSS meta-BIFs deformed mainly by dislocation creep, magnetite on multiple slip systems and with {111} twinning below 400 °C, and hematite replaced magnetite topotaxially by a redox reaction along {111}, followed by rapid recovery and weak post-replacement deformation.

decisive_move.sentence: Inferring slip systems, twinning and boundary types from EBSD misorientation and subgrain boundary trace analysis (with the new script) is what turns orientation maps into the mechanism claims.

gates.evidence: The samples were collected and scanned to describe deformation, not to test a stated hypothesis. Only the redox vs non-redox topotaxy and the tilt vs twist reading faced tests that could have failed (p. 28-29). The dislocation-creep claims rest on interpretive criteria. No analysis plan is reported as fixed in advance, and angular thresholds were adjusted per grain (p. 10).

novelty_claims.quote: The presence of distinct subgrains in magnetite, rare in natural samples, attests to the same.
dislocation creep activity in magnetite from a naturally deformed sample that has rarely been reported in the literature
this study shows that slip along 〈111〉 (Fig. 10o) and 〈100〉 (Fig. 10p) could also be possible in naturally deformed magnetite grains

limits: Three samples over a ~40 km traverse. The authors decline to relate the results to CSS-scale deformation (p. 24). Slip systems come from eight hand-picked magnetite grains of one sample (MA02), with misorientation limits varied per grain to reach 10 traces and the closest crystal direction taken as SPN/SD. This is a selection the paper does not test for bias (inference). General boundaries were excluded. Temperatures rest on published microstructural calibrations, not thermometry. Sub-claims at other statuses: the bimodal quartz grain-size origin is open (no_conclusion between pinning and precursor fabric); <111> and <100> magnetite slip directions are tentative ('could also be possible'); the cause of the inter-sample temperature heterogeneity is not explored (p. 27). The hematite MAD is shown for MA01 only. The GOS result (hematite more strained) sits uneasily with the weak post-replacement deformation claim, and the paper does not reconcile the two (inference). No review file was supplied, so referee influence cannot be coded.

disagreements.target: Hornstra (1960): 〈110〉 is the only slip direction in spinel-structured crystals
disagreements.support: Subgrain boundary trace analysis in Grains 3 and 4 gives slip directions near 〈111〉 and 〈100〉.
disagreements.quote: Although 〈110〉 is the only slip direction reported for all spinel structured crystals like [...] )

disagreements.target: Till and Moskowitz (2014): {110}〈110〉 and {100}〈110〉 slip at ≥1100 °C in laboratory magnetite
disagreements.support: {110} and {100} slip is found in natural magnetite deformed at much lower inferred temperatures.

disagreements.target: Mansard et al. (2020): orthopyroxene + plagioclase weakening requires fine-grained reaction products (800–900 °C experiments)
disagreements.support: Plastically bent orthopyroxene laths in a plagioclase porphyroclast without reaction products imply ductile behaviour below 800 °C at low strain rates.
disagreements.quote: even in the absence of an interconnected network of reaction product(s)

disagreements.target: Lagoeiro (1998): replacing hematite is dislocation-free and thus weaker
disagreements.support: The inherited hematite CPOs and low GOS are read as weak post-replacement deformation rather than weakening.
disagreements.quote: This study suggests that the post-replacement deformation, if any, was weak.
